title: AWS security assessment
description: A Terraform capstone assessed with Prowler and Security Hub, with sanitized results and a candid remediation review.
overview: I built an intentionally misconfigured AWS environment for a fictional SaaS company, assessed the findings, made targeted changes, and compared the results. The repository contains the original Terraform fixture, sanitized check aggregates, and an offline reporting tool.
details: The assessment covered S3 public-access settings, explicit encryption configuration, an open SSH rule, and IAM policy/MFA practices. The review separates configuration changes from residual risk and documents where aggregate scan scores can mislead.
outcomes: 71 → 76 passing CIS result rows; 96 → 91 failing rows.
After-scan pass rate: 45.51%, excluding 3 manual results.
Evidence aggregated without account or resource identifiers.
limitations: Historical lab, not a production engagement or a compliance certification. The new offline helper is tested locally; no live AWS resources were deployed or rescanned for this publication.

title: Azure Sentinel honeypot
description: Windows authentication telemetry, KQL investigation, GeoIP enrichment, and a Sentinel workbook showing the collected activity.
overview: I connected a Windows lab VM to Log Analytics and Microsoft Sentinel through Azure Monitor Agent and a Data Collection Rule. Failed-logon events became the starting point for investigation, enrichment, and visualization.
details: The project follows Event ID 4625 through the collection pipeline, enriches source IPs with a GeoIP watchlist, and presents the results in an attack-map workbook. The repository includes original published screenshots and reusable companion queries.
outcomes: Documented the VM → AMA/DCR → Log Analytics → Sentinel pipeline.
Used failed-logon filtering, source/account pivots, and GeoIP enrichment.
Published the workbook images and a complete walkthrough.
limitations: An isolated learning exercise inspired by Josh Madakor. Companion queries were reconstructed from the workflow and have not been re-run in a live workspace for this publication. IP geolocation does not establish attacker identity.
imageAlt: Original Microsoft Sentinel workbook map after 24 hours of the lab

title: Windows Prefetch investigation
description: A simulated-incident case study using PECmd and Timeline Explorer to reconstruct execution activity and assess investigative hypotheses.
overview: I investigated recovered Prefetch artifacts from a simulated workstation incident. The workflow anchored on a suspicious executable, examined nearby runs, and pivoted on unusual paths and referenced files.
details: The repository includes a complete investigation narrative, selected timestamp observations, command examples, and a distinction between observed execution evidence and hypotheses about collection, exfiltration, or cleanup.
outcomes: Reconstructed suspicious execution observations from a single artifact type.
Compared shared file references across several executables.
Documented the need for corroborating event, network, and filesystem evidence.
limitations: Training case based on an Eric Capuano exercise. Prefetch alone does not prove actor identity, exact commands, parent/child process relationships, or data exfiltration.
